title: The Cost of Missed Windows and the Path of Anchored Reform: A Comparative Analysis of Ethiopia’s WTO Accession Trajectory (1994–2026)
content: This paper examines the institutional, fiscal, and macroeconomic consequences of Ethiopia’s long-delayed entry into the multilateral trading system. Drawing on internal diagnostic studies and reform roadmaps submitted to the Transitional Government of Ethiopia between 1993 and 1994, the analysis reconstructs the counterfactual case for early membership. It explores how concurrent plans to roll out the Automated System for Customs Data (ASYCUDA) and establish an autonomous revenue authority were designed to resolve the classic trade-revenue dilemma. By contrasting the automatic special and differential treatment (SDT) granted to founding 1994 members under Article XI:2 of the Marrakesh Agreement with the demanding ‘WTO-Plus’ concessions required under the post-1995 Article XII accession track, the study traces the political and administrative friction behind a 23-year negotiating process. It also assesses how domestic tax policy was sequenced—specifically the shift away from border tariffs toward a domestic Value Added Tax (VAT)—alongside the heavier regulatory obligations that emerged under the Doha Development Agenda (DDA). Finally, the paper reviews how the Homegrown Economic Reform Agenda broke a decades-long stalemate, culminating in the Eighth Working Party meeting in Geneva in November 2026. Although missing the 1994 window cost Ethiopia substantial policy discretion, the Article XII process ultimately acted as an indispensable external anchor for modernising its commercial laws, foreign exchange regime, and financial sector ahead of full accession at the close of 2026.
